h1: Whisky for HR and L&D teams
title: Whisky for HR and L&D Teams | Craft Beer School
desc: How HR and L&D teams in drinks companies can run whisky product training safely: policy, responsible tastings and what to teach.
teaser: Product training in a whisky company has to teach the product without encouraging anyone to drink. L&D owns that balance.
standfirst: HR and learning teams in drinks companies face an odd brief: help people understand a product that many will not drink and some cannot. Done well, whisky training builds confidence across finance, data and sales roles. Done carelessly, it creates risk. Here is how to get the balance right.
sections: Why product training matters in support roles

A drinks company employs people far from production: analysts, planners, recruiters, engineers and finance staff. Many join from other industries. They make decisions about a product they have never seen made. That gap shows up in small ways: a forecast that ignores maturation time, a supplier switch that changes the taste or a campaign brief that ignores advertising rules.

Product training closes the gap. It explains how whisky is made, why it takes years, what the categories mean and how the Indian market works. The aim is fluency, not appreciation. Our guide to whisky for procurement teams shows how specific that fluency can be.

Before the first session, agree a written policy with legal and leadership. It should cover:

  • Participation is opt-in. Nobody is pressured or marked down for declining.
  • Nobody under the state's legal drinking age takes part. That age varies by state in India.
  • Measures are small, typically 10 to 15 ml per sample, with spit cups and water.
  • Food is served. Sessions do not run straight into driving home.
  • Pregnant colleagues, people with health or religious reasons and anyone in recovery are welcome to nose only, or skip without explanation.

The policy protects people and it protects the company. It also sets the tone: this is learning, not a party.

Most of what a whisky professional evaluates comes through the nose. Blenders typically assess samples diluted to around 20% ABV and rarely swallow. A nosing-only session teaches the same lessons: what oak adds, what sherry casks contribute, what peat smells like and how water changes aroma.

Design sessions so nosing is the default and tasting is the option. Use tulip-shaped nosing glasses with watch-glass covers if you have them. Include non-alcoholic references, such as vanilla, dried fruit, smoked foods and cereal, so everyone has an anchor. This makes the session genuinely inclusive rather than a drinking event with a token alternative.
What the core module should cover

A solid foundation module for any role covers five topics. How whisky is made, from grain to cask to bottle. The main categories: Scotch, bourbon, Irish, Indian whisky and Indian single malt. Maturation and why Indian heat changes it. How alcohol is regulated and sold in India, state by state. Responsible marketing and the limits on advertising.

Each topic should link to the company's own products and to a real number. For example, Scotch must mature at least three years in oak and be bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV. Our beginner's tasting guide works as a pre-read for people who have never tried whisky.

After the shared foundation, short role modules carry the most value. Finance learns excise, maturing stock and evaporation losses. Planning learns lead times and bottling constraints. Procurement learns specifications for spirit, casks and glass. Data teams learn litres of absolute alcohol and cask lineage. HR itself benefits from knowing which roles need deeper product skills in hiring.

Keep each role module to half a day or less. Use real company documents: a certificate of analysis, a cask inventory extract, a state label. People remember what they handled.

L&D teams need evidence. Simple measures work. A short quiz before and after on facts the role needs, such as what LAL means or why stock cannot move between states. Feedback from managers on whether escalations to production dropped. Attendance across drinkers and non-drinkers, which tells you whether the format is truly inclusive.

Avoid measuring anything about consumption. The programme succeeds when people understand the product, not when they drink more of it.
Bring the plant into the room

Training lands better when people can connect it to a place. Where the company has a distillery or bottling plant, a site visit is worth more than any slide. Walking past a fermenter, a still and a cask warehouse makes years of maturation feel real. Safety rules apply: closed shoes, no phones near ethanol vapour zones where the site forbids them and a guide at all times.

Where a visit is not practical, short videos from the company's own sites and a few physical samples (a piece of charred oak stave, malted barley, new make spirit for nosing) do much of the same job.
What your team gains from getting this right

A well-run programme gives new joiners confidence in their first months and builds respect between head office and the plant. It also signals a company culture that takes responsible drinking seriously, which matters in an industry under scrutiny.

A practical first step: draft a one-page tasting policy with your legal team, then run a nosing-only pilot with ten volunteers from different functions and ask them what they still do not understand about the product.
faqs: Should employees be required to taste whisky during training?
No. Tastings should always be opt-in. Nosing alone teaches most of what support roles need.
How much whisky is served in a training tasting?
Small measures, often 10 to 15 ml per sample, with spit cups, water and food. Follow your company policy.
What should HR include in a tasting policy?
Opt-in participation, legal age checks by state, small measures, spit cups, food, no driving afterwards and a welcome for non-drinkers.
